graduation_requirements.raw_text:
BHS students must complete a minimum of 24 credits to earn a diploma.
CREDITS REQUIRED FOR GRADUATION
4 credits English
3 credits mathematics
3 credits science
3 credits social studies (including 1 credit American History)
2 credits world language (completion of two sequential levels)
1.5 credits physical education
1 credit fine art
0.5 credits health
6 credits electives (may include annual 0.25 YES credit)
ADDITIONAL REQUIREMENTS
10 hours Community Service per year of enrollment
0.25 credit Year End Studies Program (YES) per year of enrollment
Completion of a Personalized Learning Plan (PLP)
YEAR-END STUDIES (YES)
In the fourth and final academic quarter of the school year, all students participate in the Year-End Studies (YES)
Session. Students select one full-day or two half-day, ten-day mini-courses in order to deepen learning interests
and apply academic skills and knowledge. A culminating showcase allows students, parents, and community
members to learn from each other and celebrate YES accomplishments. Students will sign up during the third
academic quarter and informed of their courses in the spring. Information on the current year’s offerings can be
found on the BHS website.
COMMUNITY SERVICE
All students must complete ten (10) hours of community service per year of enrollment at BHS. Community
service prompts students to apply their skills and knowledge locally to learn the responsibility citizens have in a
democratic society. Hours may be accrued beginning the summer preceding 9th grade through 12th grade. The
deadline to submit community service hours to confirm participation in commencement ceremonies is the last
day of Quarter 4 of the student’s graduating year. Students are responsible for tracking their hours and submitting
documentation to the School Counseling Office.
PERSONALIZED LEARNING PLAN (PLP)
In addition to academic credit accrual, students are required to develop and maintain a Personalized Learning
Plan (PLP) in order to meet graduation requirements. Students will utilize the PLP to set, review, and document
goal progress towards academic proficiencies in consultation with an advisor and their parents/guardians.
Students will collect high-quality evidence (e.g. projects, essays, performances, YES, and experiential learning) in
a digital portfolio. Students will be provided time and structure in Advisories and classroom courses to regularly
update and reflect upon this work.

courses.description: AP Computer Science A is a rigorous, college-level programming course that expands on the foundational skills learned in Computer Science 2 or 3. Students will develop proficiency in object-oriented programming using programming language Java while learning to design, implement, test, and refine software solutions to real-world problems. Key topics include creating and using classes and objects, working with complex data structures such as arrays and ArrayLists, developing algorithms that store and process data, and evaluating the efficiency and correctness of different solutions. Students will also examine broader impacts of computing, including responsible use, ethical considerations, and the social implications of software systems. The course concludes with the AP Computer Science A Exam. AP CSA is offered every other year and will run during the 2026–2027 school year.
courses.prerequisites: Teacher recommendation andearn a 80% or higher in Computer Science 2 or Computer Science 3
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Curiosity & Creativity

courses.description: Computer science touches every part of modern life, and learning to think like a computer scientist – designing solutions, writing programs, tackling challenges – gives you the power to create almost anything you can imagine. Really, it’s like a super power! This course is as much about programming and learning core computer science concepts as it is about creativity, design and problem-solving. We’ll work in Scratch, a block-based programing language ideal for complete beginners as well as those with some programming experience who want a space to explore creative computing. Most assignments project-based, with freedom to design and develop your own original programs. Students earning an 80% or higher are eligible to continue on to Computer Science 2: Programming with Python
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Curiosity & Creativity

courses.description: Physical computing forms the basis of smart devices, wearables like smart watches, e-textiles and IoT (Internet of Things) devices. In this semester course, you will learn to design electronic devices that interact with the physical world by building circuits and writing programs that run on microcontrollers (tiny, hand-held computers). You might build a robot arm that can draw, a racetrack that times the speed of a toy car, a small greenhouse that opens a vent if the temperature gets too hot – what you build is up to you! This course is project based and highly self-directed; you will have lots of freedom to pursue your own projects. We will utilize the Arduino microcontroller in projects and the programming language C++.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Computer Science II with at least an 80% or AP Computer Science A with at least a 70%; or demonstrate prior programming experience to the teacher to determine course placement
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Curiosity & Creativity

courses.description: In this course, we will learn how to design and build web pages using HTML, CSS, JavaScript and site builders. We’ll examine how thoughtful design choices improve user experience - from making sites more accessible and easier to navigate, to applying principles of visual design to create polished, visually appealing pages. During the first half of the course, we’ll focus on best practices for working with markup languages and learn how to make sites interactive with JavaScript. We’ll also explore how AI tools can support the development of more advanced features. In the second half, our attention will shift toward site builders and design. This is a project-based course with plenty of opportunities to create your own original websites. Students earning an 80% or higher are eligible to continue on to Computer Science 2: Programming with Python.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Curiosity & Creativity

courses.description: Advanced Principles of Engineering is for highly motivated students who are ready and willing to work at a faster pace with greater indepedence. Students will continue to investigate the four areas of technology education with a more in-depth physics emphasis. Students will research, design, and construct projects. Recent design challenges have included constructing parachutes, planes, maglev vehicles, electric terrain vehicles, boats, cutting boards, wooden pens and designing single color screen printing, promotional brochures, architectural layouts, and exploring alternative energy sources (wind, solar, hydro). Class will involve note taking, research, quizzes and tests, but will focus heavily on hands-on projects. This is offered every other year (2026-27, 2028-29), alternating with Principles of Engineering I (2027-28, 2029-30).

courses.description: Have you taken a design technology course and desire to expand on this learning? Do you have an idea or concept you would like to bring to life? This course is ideal for highly motivated students interested in self-directed learning in the area of design technology and STEAM. Students may choose to study a topic of their choice for a quarter or semester long independent study under the guidance of the design technology teacher. Areas of study may include, but are not limited to: photography, graphic design, architectural design (CAD), silk screen printing, 3D printing, laser technologies, and robotics.
courses.prerequisites: Recommendation of the instructor.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: During this fast-paced semester course, students will learn digital single lens reflex (D-SLR) camera operation, composition, a general history of photography, and photo manipulation through the use of Adobe Photoshop. Projects which teach correct exposure, control of movement, depth of field, photographic perception and the understanding of photographic selection and ‘framing’ will be assigned. This course will involve lectures, demonstrations, critiques and discussions with a heavy focus on hands-on projects.

courses.description: During this fast-paced semester course, students will explore the graphic design world creating 2D and 3D projects. This course will discuss the visual principles and elements of design. Basic typography, hierarchy of information, and using grid systems for layouts will also be covered. Software training will focus on Adobe Illustrator and Adobe InDesign. Students will also learn the process of silk screen process printing. Students will participate in class critiques, demonstrations, and projects. Class will involve notes, quizzes/tests, and critiques with heavy focus on hands-on projects. Knowledge of Adobe Photoshop is recommended, but not required.

courses.description: This course is for the highly motivated student wishing to obtain marketable experience in print media publishing. Students will identify and report news-making events; incorporate journalistic forms, create eye-catching layouts, and use photography to document a year in the history of Burlington High School and our community in the annual publication of our yearbook, OREAD. Students must be able to accept responsibility and work independently to meet deadlines. Documentation of events will require that yearbook class members work after school and on weekends. Upon completion of the course students will be able to 1. apply the basic principles of page design and layout 2. operate Adobe InDesign software 3. write copy for captions and text 4. shoot, select, and crop photographs for layout 5. work collaboratively to create a unified theme

Students will also learn to edit copy, lead a team to produce articles in a timely fashion, generate new story ideas and feature articles, create slideshows for school events, create marketing campaigns to continue funding the publication’s development, and assume responsibility and leadership for a certain component of the yearbook and publications.

courses.description: The 9th grade English program focuses on three core questions: Who am I? What is my community? How do I fit into the world? We practice three English reading and writing skills: annotation, speaking and listening, and evidence-based writing. This class will be co-assigned and team-taught with Humanities Civics and World Societies. Texts may include: Long Way Down by Jason Reynolds, Romeo and Juliet by William Shakespeare, Braiding Sweetgrass by Robin Wall Kimmerer, Night by Elie Wiesel, To Kill a Mockingbird by Harper Lee, and Of Mice and Men by John Steinbeck. Earned Honors: Students have the option to earn Honors credit in this class by demonstrating learning throughout the school year at an Honors level. The earned Honors designation will be awarded at the end of year and enables students to take English 10 Honors (Genre) in 10th grade.

The course will broaden students' background in reading, aid them in writing about or responding to a literary selection, and help them build their own vocabulary through the study of words in a literary context. Major works to be studied include but are not limited to: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Purple Hibiscus, A Raisin in the Sun, When the Emperor Was Divine, The Things They Carried, and Macbeth.

Students will read 60-90 pages per week, respond to texts with sensitivity, analyze elements of story and craft, write analytical essays, develop their academic vocabulary, improve their understanding of how language works, and sharpen their discussion and presentation skills. Major works may include The Things They Carried, The Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, and Macbeth. To succeed in Genre, students should be able to read and write at grade level and learn independently.

courses.description: This course introduces students to the principles and practice of journalism. Students learn what makes a good story, and how to get the facts through interviews and research. Students are in a constant process of writing and revising to create engaging and informative articles. Units include: the history and ethics of American journalism, newswriting, feature writing, opinion writing, and sports-writing. Introduction to journalism is a required course for students wishing to write for the BHS Register, the BHS print and online newspaper.

As apprentices to seasoned staff, student journalists will continue to practice the skills introduced in Introduction to Journalism. Emphasis is on research, interviewing, and rewriting to achieve mastery. New skills covered include things like digital storytelling and social media strategy. This course is only offered second semester.

The curriculum encompasses various aspects of journalism, including article writing, conducting interviews, page design, photography, advertisement design, and the creation of broadcast and social media.

courses.description: Can literature capture what it means to be an American? How does it inform our understanding of racial, class, and gender divides? These are some of the questions we will be asking as we engage with a variety of texts spanning the previous century. We will look at poetry, short stories, and novels from the era, placing them in their larger historical and cultural contexts. Close reading and writing will be emphasized throughout the semester. We will study literature with the assumption that art both shapes and reflects culture. Some writers we may read include F. Scott Fitzgerals, Jack Kerouac, and Toni Morrison.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking and Problem Solving, Curiosity and Creativity, Effective Communication.

courses.description: This course offers an introduction to African American literature. Students will read and engage with poetry, short stories, essays, and novels written by African American writers from varied time periods and literary movements as they look for how these texts relate, converse, revise, or depend upon each other. Students will evaluate essays, poems, and novels written by writers such as Zora Neale Hurston, Maya Angelou, James Baldwin, Ta-Nehisi Coates, Toni Morrison and Octavia Butler. We will respond to the works we study with academic essays and creative projects.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of 10th grade English.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

courses.description: Students explore the darker aspects of human nature through 19th century American stories about the influence of evil, self righteousness, and psychological angst. These worlds are often haunted by female heroines, supernatural elements, and the fears born out of the beginnings of a new nation.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of 10th grade English.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

courses.description: The AP English Language and Composition course focuses on the development and revision of evidence-based analytic and argumentative writing, the rhetorical analysis of nonfiction texts, and the decisions writers make as they compose and revise. Students evaluate, synthesize, and cite research to support their arguments. Additionally, they read and analyze rhetorical elements and their effects in nonfiction-- including images as forms of texts-- from a range of disciplines and historical periods.This course provides preparation for the AP examination in AP English Language and Composition.
courses.prerequisites: Teacher Recommendation. Completion of a summer assignment is required for enrollment in this course.

courses.description: This year-long course is designed for students who want to expand their awareness of language, strengthen their critical reading of poetry and fiction, and further develop their writing style. To understand the power of the written word students will be reading and evaluating the works of established writers, while also writing and evaluating their own writing using the writing process of drafting, editing and revising. Students will be active readers as well as writers, engaging in thoughtful discussions about the role of the writer and the individual in an ever-changing world. This course is concerned with the individual's search for identity, embracing not just the issue of freedom, but also the problems of responsibility and commitment. Novels, short stories, poems and essays are used to examine the themes of fate and free will, illusion and reality, the nature of justice and the question of identity. While examining such themes, students will read critically to determine an author’s purpose, audience, literary strategies, and style and provide evidence of their understanding through class discussions and writings. Students should expect to read and write extensively in this This course provides preparation for the AP examination in English Literature and course. Composition. Major works to be studied may include but are not limited to: Man's Search for Meaning, Blood Dazzler, Slaughterhouse Five, Crime and Punishment, Frankenstein, One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, The Stranger, Waiting for Godot, Beloved, and Invisible Man. Students taking this course are able to demonstrate the ability to do college level work by analyzing literature in depth and writing multiple essays of analysis. Completion of a summer assignment is required for enrollment in this course.

courses.description: What makes a great movie? Cinema Studies provides the tools to understand and analyze films. We’ll learn about the ways that directors decide on the camera work, set and costume design, and editing to bring their visions to the screen. We will watch films by a variety of directors, each with their own style and approach to storytelling. We will look at how movies have evolved over time. We will analyze camera angles, lighting, sound, and read and write movie reviews. Projects may include storyboarding films, staging photographs to replicate common camera angles and techniques, studying and reviewing a film or a series of films independently, and completing an analysis of a movie’s techniques and values.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Effective Communication

courses.description: This course provides students with opportunities to improve and expand their writing skills. Students will develop an awareness of language, read with more critical understanding, and develop an individual writing style. Writing is a process, which involves prewriting, drafting, revising, and editing. Correct grammar and effective language are a focus of the course. Students read and analyze essays of narration, description, process analysis, comparison and contrast, division and classification, definition, cause and effect, and persuasion and argument. Then, they write their own essays in these styles. This class becomes a writing community where students share and discuss ideas, thoughts, and works. The main focus of this class is writing, but we will also address standards and benchmarks of reading and writing, with an emphasis on writing clear, concise papers that reflect the proper use of the conventions of English.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Curiosity and Creativity; Personal Development.

courses.description: Contemporary literature is often defined as “post-war” (WWII). In this class, students will explore contemporary literature by examining the human experience through texts that belong to and speak to the present. Students drive the lines of inquiry and will read poetry, short stories, and novels, and watch films to gain a deeper understanding of the human condition today. Course proficiencies focus on critical thinking, close reading, and creativity. Students will keep a journal, share their writing and thinking, and formally present their understanding. Units of study may include: post-apocalyptic literature, postmodern storytelling techniques, and a choice-read unit. Core texts may include but are not limited to The Road and Memento.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking and Problem Solving, Curiosity and Creativity, Effective Communication.

courses.description: How do we effectively craft and tell stories? This semester long course is aimed at developing creative writing skills through composition, critique, and revision in an intensive workshop format. Students will explore writing as a process while also sharpening the ability to evaluate creative writings. Students will create short stories, poems, plays, and more. As a class, we will work toward understanding the purposes and motives behind writing. The elements and techniques that go into an effective piece will be constantly analyzed and discussed so that students will perceive some of the various formulas authors use to create immortal, effective art. Students will post and publish work online and in print to reach a wide variety of audiences.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication, Curiosity & Creativity.

courses.description: This course examines books, speeches, movies, documentaries, and other forms of media centered around topics which have inspired fear in Americans. Through in-depth discussions, we will unpack the role that fear has played in shaping American culture, and attempt to understand the core fears upon which these topics are hinged. Students will practice analytical writing, creative writing and dialogue. Units of study may include War of the Worlds (radio broadcast), Poltergeist, The Bad Seed, Skeleton Crew, “The Lottery,” Psycho, Interview with a Vampire, Baby Teeth, Black Mirror,Twilight Zone, The Final Girl Support Group, The Blair Witch Project, and The Amityville Horror.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical thinking and problem solving, curiosity and creativity

courses.description: This elective course is designed to give students an in-depth look at both the reading and writing of poetry. Students will examine works by established poets from various movements and cultures throughout the ages. Students will study poetic language, symbolism and themes, as well as voice, style and purpose. Students will engage in reading, reciting and analyzing poetry, as well as creating their own original, poetic works, which will be first edited by a conference partner and then shared with the class upon completion. Proficiency in these areas will be assessed throughout the course.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Curiosity and Creativity; Civic Engagement & Cross-Cultural Understanding.

courses.description: This course will include reading, discussion, and written analysis of several major plays and some of the sonnets. The course explores Shakespeare’s challenging language and the memorable characters that populate his works, including kings, queens, lovers, shrews and fools. Themes such as power, revenge, love, jealousy, ambition and betrayal will be discussed. Critical approaches including psychological, feminist, and historical theories may be presented and applied to the texts.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Creativity and Curiosity, Personal Development

courses.description: Speech class will help students to become more effective and confident public speakers. This class offers students the opportunity to learn the fundamentals of public speaking and to study the basics of communication theory. Students will develop individual speaking styles and study the intricacies of effective speech and improve their writing through a process that includes pre-writing, drafting, revising, and editing. Students will choose their own topics to write with purpose: to inform, to entertain, to argue, and to persuade. Students will also address standards of reading, as we study speeches from history and communication theory. This class values creating a writing community where students openly share and discuss ideas, thoughts, and works.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Personal Development.

courses.description: In this course, you’ll explore how stories work and why they matter to us. We’ll read a wide range of fiction, from classic and contemporary writers like Alice Walker, Octavia Butler, and Samanta Schweblin. You’ll learn how characters develop, how authors build themes, and how point of view shapes meaning. You’ll practice close reading, collaborative annotation, and literary interpretation using different lenses such as feminist, psychological, or historical. Through discussions, writing, and media, you’ll strengthen your critical thinking and discover how stories connect to your own life and identity.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical thinking and problem solving; Effective Communication.

courses.description: Students read and discuss literature about and by women who have investigated, challenged, and shaped notions of womanhood. This is a survey course. Students read challenging essays, plays, poems, short stories, articles, and novels. Students write extensively, and engage in seminar-style class discussions in this college-preparatory level class. Texts may include Passing by Nella Larsen, The Bluest Eye by Toni Morrison, Woman Warrior by Maxine Hong Kingston, and The Awakening by Kate Chopin.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical thinking and problem solving; Effective Communication

courses.description: World Literature investigates global cultural perspectives about universal human ideas like forgiveness, family, truth, and what it really means “to live a good life.” We will read books and watch films from diverse world creators based on their culture, compare them to each other, and to our own cultural perspective. This is a writing and discussion-based course that will focus on analysis and comparison of ideas, asking you to become cultural investigators and appreciators of perspectives very different from your own.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement Department of Multilingual Learners

courses.description: This course provides basic language instruction to new English language speakers in all four domains. This class is designed for EL students who have very limited English proficiency.
courses.prerequisites: ELP Levels 1-2.

courses.description: This initial reading course provides newcomer students instruction in the foundations of literacy in English. Students will learn the English phonetic systems, early literacy skills, and language needed to continue reading courses at Burlington High School. Students will develop basic reading and comprehension skills.
courses.prerequisites: ELP Levels 1-2.

courses.description: This course develops background knowledge of natural processes and basic scientific concepts, principles, theory, methods, and essential vocabulary. A hands-on approach will be used to establish comprehension.
courses.prerequisites: ELP Levels 1-2 .

courses.description: The goal of this course is to develop background knowledge of world geography and cultures. Students will focus on developing a comprehension of and use of concepts and skills necessary for reading primary sources and non-fiction texts, writing evidence based paragraphs, creating presentations of learning, and participating in research activities in social studies. Social studies concepts will be introduced such as concepts of historical past, timelines and chronology, geographical terms, map usage terms, economic terms, role of culture and concepts of tradition. The proficiencies introduced in this course mirrors the ninth grade social studies proficiencies to facilitate students moving into the mainstream after achieving a foundation of English language and social studies skills.
courses.prerequisites: ELP Levels 2.

courses.description: The goal of this course is to provide basic direct reading instruction to beginning English language learners. This course is designed to assist students in developing English language reading skills. Upon successful completion of Reading 1, and depending on English and language skill proficiency, students will take Supplemental Reading, Lexia, or Reading 2 classes.
courses.prerequisites: ELP Levels 1-2 and/or Lexile level BR0-L100.

courses.description: Year 1 and 2. This is a skills-based class that will focus on strengthening the foundations of reading: decoding, fluency, reading comprehension, and vocabulary. This course will include opportunities for whole class discussions and collaboration, small group work, and independent practice. Everyone can become a better, more successful reader and the goal for this course is to provide the skills and strategies that students can apply across settings to improve their reading and understanding of text. This course will run for a half block each day.
courses.prerequisites: ML Department Recommendation, IXL 0-200, review of SRI Scores and testing data
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication

courses.description: The goal of this course is to provide language instruction to English language learners in order to continue to develop students’ English language proficiency in all four language domains of reading, writing, speaking and listening in English. Prerequisite: ELP Level 2.

Students in this course develop background knowledge of U.S. History and Government. Students will focus on developing a comprehension of and use of concepts and skills necessary for reading non-fiction texts and primary sources, writing evidence based paragraphs and participating in research activities in mainstream social studies courses. Students will learn terms related to historical past, timelines and chronology, geography, map usage, economy, government, culture, and concepts of tradition, heritage, history, immigration and migration, freedom, and slavery. This course is designed to meet American History standards for those students who enter BHS having not had an American History class.
courses.prerequisites: ELP Level 2.

courses.description: This course provides reading instruction to English language learners to further develop their English language reading skills. Students will develop vocabulary and writing skills while reading increasingly complex texts.
courses.prerequisites: ELP Level 2 and/or Lexile level BR0-300.

courses.description: The goal of this course is to develop background knowledge of the natural processes as well as the basic scientific concepts, principles, theory, method and essential vocabulary to English learners who lack an educational background or the language necessary for mainstream science. Students in this class will continue to use a hands-on approach to establish comprehension.
courses.prerequisites: ELP Level 2-3. INTERMEDIATE ENGLISH Levels 3-5

courses.description: This course provides language instruction to English learners at an ELP proficiency level 3, in order to advance their development of English in all four language domains and to help students prepare for mainstream English classes. This course will build upon those skills learned in EL English 2.
courses.prerequisites: ELP Writing Level 3.

courses.description: This course provides reading instruction to English language learners to further develop their English language reading skills. Students will develop vocabulary, morphology and comprehension skills while reading increasingly complex texts.
courses.prerequisites: ELP Level 3 and/or Lexile level 200-500.

courses.description: The goal of this course is to provide language instruction to English language learners at a Proficiency Level 3.5 to 4, further advance ELs academic English skills in all four language domains, and help students transition to mainstream English classes. This course also focuses on the 9th and 10th grade English proficiencies of annotating, summarizing and speaking. This course will build upon those skills learned in English Language 3.
courses.prerequisites: ELP Writing Level 4.

courses.description: This class is a support class for English language learners concurrently enrolled in the co-taught 9th grade Humanities and Earth Science. This course will provide students with additional language instruction necessary to succeed in English 9/ Humanities and Earth Science, as well as continue to develop and refine English language skills in speaking, listening, reading, and writing. Placement will be based on reading assessments and will be based on ELL ACCESS scores.
courses.prerequisites: Enrollment in 9th grade Humanities/Civics/Earth Science. ELP Level 3-5.

courses.description: This class supports EL students also enrolled in World History and Biology or Chemistry in order to provide additional instruction, vocabulary and language development, and research assistance to ensure student academic success in mainstream history and science classes.
courses.prerequisites: Enrollment in World History or Biology ELP Level 3.5-5, or other science elective.

courses.description: This supported EL introduction to science course emphasizes laboratory skills and safety. Basic chemistry concepts including matter, compounds, chemical bonding, chemical equations and chemical reactions are included in this course.
courses.prerequisites: ELP Levels 3-4.
courses.notes: Also listed on p.92 of main catalog as 'Introduction to Chemistry' (Science & Technology); text differs from this entry; prerequisite there: Successful completion of Science 2 or equivalent and/or WIDA Level 2-3

courses.description: This course develops background knowledge on the five units in Health Education: Mental Health, Nutrition, Substance Abuse, Relationships and Sexuality. There is a specific focus on concepts, principles, and essential vocabulary. This class is designed for EL students who have limited English proficiency.
courses.prerequisites: ELP Levels 2-3

courses.course_name: College & Career Readiness for Multilingual Learners
courses.description: This course helps multilingual students prepare for life after high school by exploring college options, career pathways, and workplace expectations. Students build academic English while practicing real-world skills such as goal-setting, resume writing, interviewing, and navigating applications and financial aid. By the end of the course, students create a personalized plan for their post-secondary goals.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: This course builds speaking and communication skills for English language learners. Students practice real-world and academic communication through discussions, presentations, and collaborative activities.
courses.prerequisites: Teacher Recommendation

courses.description: This introductory singing class is designed for students with little to no formal music ensemble or singing experience. This course is a space for EL students as well as students who have never seen sheet music or made music in a formal group setting before to learn the fundamentals of singing through a variety of songs and genres in a slow-paced, student-driven, and supportive group environment.

AP 2D Art and Design is a portfolio driven course where students create a collection of artwork and designs showing both technical skill and individual creative exploration. Using a variety of different media and techniques students will explore their ideas in a year long creative journey. Students will be exposed to advanced 2D Art and Design concepts and will keep a year-long sketchbook. Students must bring creative forces and imagination to their own education and development. These qualities are encouraged and stimulated through open ended assignments and refined through class interaction and critique. Students should be prepared to make and talk about art both on a philosophical and conceptual level. This course is ideal for students who are self-driven, want to challenge themselves, or are creating a portfolio for college applications. AP 2D Art and Design is a rigorous course and requires an exceptional work ethic.
courses.prerequisites: 4 semesters of art courses AND portfolio / permission of instructor
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem

courses.description: AP Drawing is a portfolio driven course where students create a collection of artwork and designs showing both technical drawing skill and individual creative exploration. Using a variety of different media and techniques students will explore their ideas in a year long creative journey. Students must bring creative forces and imagination to their own education and development. These qualities are encouraged and stimulated through open ended assignments and refined through class interaction and critique. Students should be prepared to make and talk about art both on a philosophical and conceptual level. This course is ideal for students who are self-driven, want to challenge themselves, or are creating a portfolio for college applications. AP Drawing is a rigorous course and requires an exceptional work ethic.
courses.prerequisites: 4 semesters of art courses AND portfolio / permission of instructor
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: AP Art History is an introductory college-level art history course. Students cultivate their understanding of art history through analyzing works of art and placing them in historical context as they explore concepts like culture and cultural interactions, theories and interpretations of art, the impact of materials, processes, and techniques on art and art making, and understanding purpose and audience in art historical analysis.
courses.prerequisites: 1 Credit of Visual Art
courses.notes: Student cap: 20 | Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.course_name: Art Foundations (Formerly known as Art I)
courses.description: This semester-long studio course is designed to provide students with the foundational knowledge and skills to practice the creative process of creating, presenting, responding, and connecting through the visual arts. Students will strengthen their discipline literacy of the elements of art as they explore a variety of media, techniques, and design concepts. This course will develop creative thinking and problem solving skills, observational skills, and build self-expression and reflection. Art Foundations is a prerequisite for all upper level art classes.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: This is an introductory ceramics course focused primarily on building foundational skills in hand-building and supplemented by opportunities to explore basic wheel-throwing techniques. Students will learn pinch pot, coil and slab construction methods, as well as surface decoration, glazing processes and safe studio practices. Through guided practice and projects, students will gain an understanding of the properties of clay, the stages of the ceramic process, and the artistic possibilities of working in three dimensions.
courses.prerequisites: Successful Completion of Art Foundations (formerly known as Art I)
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity, Critical Thinking & Problem Solving

courses.description: This is an intermediate course for students who wish to further develop their skills. Students will advance their hand-building abilities, strengthen wheel-throwing techniques, and explore a range of surface treatments and glazing methods. The course emphasizes refined craftsmanship, creative problem-solving, and the development of personal artistic style.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Ceramics I
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity, Critical Thinking & Problem Solving

courses.description: Drawing 1 is an introductory studio art course that teaches the essential skills of observational and creative drawing. Students explore line, value, proportion, shading, and perspective while working with a variety of mediums. Projects emphasize the elements of art and principles of design, encouraging both technical growth and personal expression. Students will also learn basic critique skills and study selected artists for inspiration. By the end of the course, each student will develop a small portfolio demonstrating improved technique and creativity.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Art Foundations (formerly known as Art I)
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: Drawing 2 is an intermediate, studio-based course designed to continue building students’ skills in drawing. Through hands-on practice, students will learn the essential techniques, concepts, and processes used in observational and imaginative drawing. Drawing 2 will be encouraged to find and practice their own style while applying the elements of art and principles of design to demonstrate their understanding of visual literacy. In addition to studio work, students will develop their ability to critique artwork, reflect on their creative choices, and discuss artistic techniques using appropriate vocabulary. By the end of the course, students will have a portfolio of finished drawings that demonstrate technical growth, creativity, and problem-solving.
courses.prerequisites: Drawing I
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: This introductory studio course in Fiber Arts explores natural and synthetic fiber materials as the primary media to create sculptural artworks. Students will explore a variety of fibers and fiber techniques, focusing on elements of art, principles of design, historical context, and applying it to their own creative expression. Students will study fiber artists and their works, culminating in hands-on projects, critical analysis, and exhibition of their own artworks. Students will build technical skills and vocabulary to successfully pursue upper level fiber art courses.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Art Foundations (formerly known as Art I)
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity, Critical Thinking & Problem Solving

courses.description: In this intermediate-level course, students explore a selection of diverse concepts, materials, and processes associated with contemporary fiber arts. Emphasis will be on defining the line between craft and fine art, expanding conceptual development as well as furthering students' technical skills. The course will address the process and development of transforming ideas into form, and pushing the boundaries of traditional craft for visual storytelling.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Fiber Arts I
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity, Critical Thinking & Problem Solving

courses.course_name: Mixed Media I (Formerly known as Art II)
courses.description: This is a studio course that introduces students to the combined use of drawing, painting, collage and digital media. Students will develop technical skills and creative problem-solving techniques as they explore how multiple materials and processes can be integrated into cohesive artworks. Coursework emphasizes composition, material experimentation, and thoughtful artistic decision-making. By the end of the course, students will complete a portfolio of original mixed-media pieces and gain a deeper understanding of how diverse media can be used to communicate ideas and personal expression.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Drawing I or Painting I
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.course_name: Mixed Media II (Formerly known as Art II)
courses.description: This course builds on foundational mixed media skills to help students develop a more personal and sophisticated artistic voice. Through layered exploration of drawing, painting, collage, printmaking, sculpture and digital processes, students learn to combine materials with intention and craftsmanship. Emphasis is placed on creative problem-solving, concept development, experimentation and refining technical skills.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Mixed Media I
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: Painting 1 is an introductory art course that teaches students the basic skills and techniques of painting. Students learn how to use different painting materials—such as acrylics and watercolors—and explore fundamental concepts like color theory, composition, and brushwork. The class includes guided projects that help students develop creativity, observation skills, and confidence in their artistic abilities.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Art Foundations (formerly known as Art I)
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: Painting 2 is an intermediate course designed for students who have completed Painting I and want to deepen their artistic skills. Students explore more advanced techniques in acrylic, watercolor, and mixed media while studying color harmony, style, and personal expression. Projects encourage creativity, problem-solving, and the development of a personal artistic voice. Emphasis is placed on refining technique, experimenting with new approaches, and building a strong portfolio.
courses.prerequisites: Painting I
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: Printmaking is an introductory art course that teaches students how to create images using a variety of printmaking techniques. Students explore methods such as relief printing, monoprinting, and collagraphs while learning about design, craftsmanship, and safe studio practices. The course emphasizes creativity, experimentation, and developing strong visual ideas.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Art Foundations (formerly known as Art I)
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: Sculpture 1 is an introductory studio course in three-dimensional (3D) art making. Students will explore a variety of sculpture techniques with diverse media, including found materials, focusing on elements of art, principles of design, historical context, and applying it to their own creative expression. Students will study sculptors and their works, culminating in hands-on projects, critical analysis, and exhibition of their own artworks. Students will build skills and vocabulary to successfully pursue upper level sculpture courses.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Art Foundations (formerly known as Art I)
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: In this intermediate-level course, students explore a selection of diverse concepts, materials, and processes associated with contemporary sculpture. Students will experience a variety of additive and subtractive sculpture techniques through various media. Emphasis will be on exploring alternative methods of art production, expanding conceptual development as well as furthering students' technical skills. The course will address the process and development of transforming ideas into form.
courses.prerequisites: Sculpture I
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: This introductory guitar class is designed for students with diverse abilities and little or no guitar experience. Utilizing guitars provided by the school and adaptive techniques, students will learn the fundamentals of playing, reading, and writing guitar music in an inclusive and supportive environment.
courses.prerequisites: School-based team referral required.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: This course is designed for students who are curious about how music really works, how melodies are built, how harmonies fit together, and what gives music its structure and meaning. AP Music Theory introduces the foundations of harmony and melody as the first year of a college-level music theory sequence. Students begin with essential skills such as note and rhythm reading, intervals, and scales, and then progress to harmonies, chord progressions, ear training, melodic analysis, and composition. By the end of the year, students are prepared to take the Advanced Placement exam, which may allow them to earn college credit, skip a year of college music theory, and/or receive fine arts credit—giving them a strong head start in their musical journey. Successful students typically enter the course with some musical background and basic note-reading skills in at least one clef. While it is strongly encouraged that students in BHS performing ensembles continue in those classes alongside AP Music Theory, since each course supports and strengthens the other, students who are not in a performing ensemble may still enroll and succeed in AP Music Theory. This course is offered every other year (2026-27, 2028-29 etc.).
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Music Appreciation (formerly known as Music Theory), one of the ensemble classes, or instructor permission.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving. | *BHS partners with Saint Michael’s College to offer this course as a concurrent enrollment class. This means that you could earn college credit for this class, in addition to BHS credit. If a student opts in concurrent college enrollment for this course, they will need to submit a dual enrollment voucher form to Saint Michael’s. See Ms. Stein (kstein@bsdvt.org) for details and support. | Also listed on p.112 of main catalog as 'AP Music Theory' (Flexible Pathways) | Concurrent enrollment option (p.110): BHS partners with St. Michael’s College (SMC) to offer college credit for the equivalent of AP US Government, AP Literature, Honors Physics and AP Music Theory.

courses.description: The Chamber Choir is a select auditioned group that meets weekly before school hours to sing music scored for smaller ensembles. Students will sing Soprano/Alto, Tenor/Bass, and SATB pieces. The group rehearses music from many different genres (acapella, barbershop, musical theater, madrigals, and more) in preparation for several performances during the school year. A strong commitment must be made to rehearsals and to work outside of the regular rehearsal period.
courses.prerequisites: Audition or recommendation from Choir Director is required.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Personal Development, Curiosity & Creativity.

courses.description: The Concert Band presents and encourages music performance at Burlington High School. The Concert Band is open to all students in grades 10-12 who play woodwind, brass, or percussion instruments. The Concert Band studies music from many different historical periods presenting diverse musical styles and genres. This performance ensemble is dedicated to the development of individual instrumental technique and large ensemble skills. Students are eligible to represent Burlington High School through music festivals at the district, state, and regional levels.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of 1 year of Freshman Band
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: The Concert Choir is open to ninth grade and other new singers who wish to participate in the BHS choral program. In addition to performances, members in this group will engage in a program designed to improve their musical skills in rhythm, reading, and technical proficiency on their voice part. This course will include the study of music theory, rehearsal procedure, proper practice habits and a variety of aspects to help strengthen vocal skills. All students interested in singing are encouraged to sign up for this course, even if you do not presently sing.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: Calling all string players! The Concert Orchestra is open to all students in grades 9-12 who play violin, viola, cello or string bass. In Concert Orchestra, we study and perform works from the classical genre as well as music from movies, musicals and more! In addition to instruction on their instruments, students will also have brief lessons in music history and music theory to help them become a well rounded musician. Students are eligible to represent Burlington High School through music festivals at the state and regional levels. Instruments are provided for those in need.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: Digital Music is an introductory course open to all students regardless of music experience. This course is an introduction to the integration of electronics into the world of music creation. Students are taught how to utilize a digital audio workstation, to remix pre existing pieces of music as well as create their own projects from scratch. Students will also be introduced to podcasting and the art of cinema composition. Additionally, students will study composition and recording techniques used by today’s most popular recording artists.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Personal Development, Curiosity & Creativity, Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: The Freshmen Band presents and encourages music performance at Burlington High School. The Concert Band is open to all students in grade 9 who play woodwind, brass, or percussion instruments. The Freshmen Band studies music from many different historical periods presenting diverse musical styles and genres. This performance ensemble is dedicated to the development of individual instrumental technique and large ensemble skills. Students are eligible to represent Burlington High School through music festivals at the district, state, and regional levels.
courses.prerequisites: All students welcome

courses.description: This introductory guitar class is designed for students with little or no guitar experience. Using guitars provided by the school, students will learn the basics of playing, reading, and writing guitar music. In this course, students will play notes and melodies through the range of the instrument, learn about 20 chords, and read music in standard notation, pop chord notation, and tablature. Music will be chosen from folk, classical, rock, and popular styles.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: This advanced guitar class is designed for 10th-12th grade students with experience playing guitar and reading music. Students will continue to improve their reading, writing, and playing skills. They will be introduced to playing in different positions, barre chords, transposition, and ensemble playing. Music will be chosen from folk, classical, rock, and popular styles. Students who have not taken Guitar I should discuss this choice with a guidance counselor or music teacher before enrolling.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Guitar I or teacher recommendation.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: An introduction to the art and practice of theatre, including acting, directing, stage managing, playwriting, and the various design elements (scenic (set), lighting, sound, wardrobe, and more). This exploratory course will utilize Burlington High School's state of the art performing arts space. This course provides a balanced creative and technical theater education for students of any experience level.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: The Jazz Ensemble presents and encourages music performance at Burlington High School. This yearlong co-curricular group meets twice a week in the morning before school and is open to band and orchestra members. Repertoire includes classic big band charts as well as arrangements by contemporary artists. There is a strong emphasis on jazz styles and improvisation. Students are eligible to represent Burlington High School at the Vermont All-State Festival.
courses.prerequisites: Audition required. Auditions are open to students presently enrolled in: concert band, wind ensemble, string orchestra, or symphonic strings (exceptions for guitar and piano only).
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.course_name: Music Appreciation (Formerly Introduction to Music Theory I)
courses.description: This course aims to deepen student’s appreciation of music through the study of historical context, music theory, and song writing. Current events, pop culture, and students' music preferences are the driving force for this course. Western Classical music will be used to introduce foundational musical concepts such as reading music in different clefs, learning scales, and basic music composition and notation. This course is appropriate for musicians at any level. You are not required to play an instrument or perform in a music ensemble.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: This Piano I class meets students where they are at in their piano journey, whether that is a brand new beginner, or a student who has dabbled in piano before and looking for more experience. Using keyboards provided by the school, students will learn the basics of playing, reading, and/or writing piano music. In this course, students will learn to play songs designed for their level, chords, melodies and read music in standard notation. Music will be chosen from folk, classical, and popular styles. Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving

This intermediate piano class is designed for students with experience playing piano and reading music. Students will continue to improve their reading, writing, and playing skills. They will be introduced to playing in different keys, scales and arpeggios and further study of basic music theory.. Music will be chosen from folk, classical, rock, and popular styles. Students who have not taken Piano I should discuss this choice with their school counselor or music teacher before enrolling.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Piano I or teacher recommendation.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: The Senior Choir is open to students who like singing in mixed voices (soprano/alto/tenor/bass) and are committed to improving their vocal development. Music of all styles will be performed and studied while giving proper attention to singing technique, music reading, analysis, and evaluation. Exploration of world music will also be offered. Students who wish to play a more active part in their choral development are offered the opportunity to audition for the following music festivals: Champlain Valley District, Vermont All State, and New England Music Festivals. In addition to the scheduled performances each year, students will also be given the opportunity to perform in several Small Ensemble Performances.
courses.prerequisites: One year of Concert Choir or recommendation of the instructor.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: Calling all advancing string players! The Symphonic Orchestra is open to all students in grades 10-12 who play violin, viola, cello or string bass. Symphonic Orchestra students will study and perform more advanced works from the classical genre as well as music from movies, musicals and more! In addition to instruction on their instruments, students will also have brief lessons in higher level music history and music theory to help them become a well rounded musician. Students are eligible to represent Burlington High School through music festivals at the state and regional levels. Instruments are provided for those in need.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Concert Orchestra or recommendation of instructor.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving, Personal Development.

courses.description: Wind Ensemble presents and encourages music performance at Burlington High School. Wind Ensemble is open to students in grades 10-12 who play woodwind, brass, or percussion instruments. Performance repertoire will include masterworks for the wind band and advanced 20th century compositions. Emphasis is placed on independence of parts, technical proficiency, and musical interpretation. A minimum of one year’s experience in Concert Band is strongly recommended. Students are eligible to represent Burlington High School through music festivals at the district, state, and regional levels.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of 1 year of Freshman Band or Concert Band.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: This year-long course, coordinated with Humanities English 9, will explore the themes of power, liberty, security and conflict. Our examinations of these themes will be filtered through the lens of American government and culture, and will also include global differences and impact. Students are expected to demonstrate their understanding of how our democratic republic functions and their roles and responsibilities as citizens. In addition, students examine issues and Constitutional protections connected to human rights. We will also consider global geography, politics, economics, Students have the option to earn Honors status and culture, including religion, in the study of history. in this class by demonstrating learning of core concepts, skills, and knowledge on identified assignments and assessments during the school year at an honors level. The earned honors designation will be awarded at the end of the year. This class is co-assigned and team-taught with English 9: Humanities.
courses.fulfills_text: History dept table: 9th Required (3.0 Credits Required)
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Personal Development; and Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

courses.description: Uncover the complexities of our world in this college preparatory course, offering insights into significant events, ideas, individuals, and institutions that have shaped our global narrative. Beyond exploring historical accounts, this course equips you with vital study and critical thinking skills essential for success at the college level. Delve into a diverse array of readings and resources, including both primary and secondary materials, presenting conflicting interpretations. Embrace the challenge of approaching historical questions analytically and critically.
courses.fulfills_text: History dept table: 10th Required (World History or World History Honors)
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Personal Development; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

courses.description: This course is designed to challenge students to study World History in depth, with emphasis on central questions, problems, causes, decisions and interpretations. Students will think about and discuss forces, issues, ideas, themes and problems in the world. Wide and varied readings and resources both primary and secondary will be used. They will present conflicting interpretations and students will be encouraged to deal with historical questions analytically and critically. Students are expected to have strong reading and writing skills.
courses.prerequisites: Earned honors in Humanities: Civics and World Societies
courses.fulfills_text: History dept table: 10th Required (World History or World History Honors)
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Personal Development; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

courses.description: This course fulfills 1.0 credits of the American History graduation requirement Drawing from the expertise and experience of college faculty and teachers across the country, the course is designed to offer high school students an evidence-based introduction to African American studies. The interdisciplinary course reaches into a variety of fields of literature, the arts and humanities, political science, geography, and science to explore the vital contributions and experiences of African Americans. “A solid understanding of how African Americans have shaped America, its history, laws, institutions, culture and arts, and even the current practice of American democracy, sharpens all knowledge about our nation” (Dr. Nikki Taylor, Chair of the Howard University History Department). This course fulfills 1.0 credits of the American History graduation requirement.
courses.prerequisites: B or higher in World History or World History Honors or AP World History, teacher recommendation, and completion of a summer reading and writing assignment.
courses.fulfills_text: This course fulfills 1. This course fulfills 1. | History dept table: 11th Required - one year of an American History course in an Advanced Placement course
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking and Problem Solving; Cultural Understanding and Civic Engagement; Effective Communication; Curiosity and Creativity; and Personal Development.

courses.description: This course fulfills 1.0 credits of the American History graduation requirement This course is a college level survey in United States History that covers the Age of Exploration through to the present. Content covers the political, social/cultural, economic, and diplomatic events and how they collectively have contributed to the development of the United States. Drawing from the expertise and experience of college faculty and teachers across the country, the course is designed to offer high school students an evidence-based introduction to United States History. This is a semester-based course that provides an opportunity to explore American History through the voices that are often silenced, such as Native Americans, European immigrants, and Latinos. We aim to unpack the social, political and economic implications on America’s development on marginalized peoples in an ethnic studies approach. Our historical timeline of study is from First Contact through Reconstruction. This course has been designed and inspired by historian Howard Zinn’s book, “A People’s History of the United States.” We use both primary and secondary sources to support our learning. Ultimately, the goal is to broaden our understanding of what it means to be a citizen in the United States, as narratives and perspectives have been left unheard. In order to fully appreciate the complex history of this nation, it is vital to recognize all voices that have played a part in America’s development, including their arduous journey.

courses.description: This course fulfills 0.5 credits of the American History graduation requirement. This is a course about America's history through the lens of labor. We will explore the role that organized labor has played in the development of the US and examine the changing nature of work, worker movements, and employment relations in the United States. This is ultimately a US history survey course that seeks to take the lens of labor to cover key moments of US history from its founding to the present day. We will explore and analyze the attitudes, ideologies, cultures, and politics of workers, labor leaders, and employers. This course will also examine how workers of different national, ethnic, racial, and gender backgrounds have experienced work and contributed to the development of unions and worker movements. Other important themes include the rights and responsibilities of employers and workers, the role of the state in the economy and the workplace, the rise and decline of collective bargaining and the New Deal order, globalization and neoliberalism, and the current problems facing workers and the emergence of new worker movements.

Embracing the thematic approach of AP World History, learners will uncover connections across time and space, examining themes such as interaction between humans and the environment, the development and interaction of cultures, and the impact of technology and innovation. courses.description: A general survey course designed to introduce students to major themes in African history. The course focuses on colonialism and decolonization, nationalism and self-liberation, development and neocolonialism, as well as African experiences of independence and every day in our contemporary, global world. Taking a chronological and thematic approach, this course explores major themes in African history from the end of the slave trade to contemporary times. We will cover materials from North, South, East, West, and Central Africa and explore connections between Africa and the rest of the world. Discussions will explore themes ranging from gender, age, class, race, and ethnicity, and the legacies of history in “modern” Africa. The course uses a variety of primary and secondary sources, including essays, films, photographs, speeches, newspaper articles, and political documents.

The course will therefore be vigorous in its study of current events, but will also rely heavily on individual students to add value to the traditional economic curriculum.
