The course will cover topics such as exponential and logarithmic functions, trigonometric functions, analytic trigonometry, applications of trigonometric functions, polar coordinates, analytic geometry (conic sections), sequences and series, binomial theorem, counting and probability, and the idea of limits. Students will be provided with graphing calculators to use in class.
courses.prerequisites: Final grade of B+ or higher in Honors Algebra II, a final grade of A in Algebra II, or teacher recommendation.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Curiosity & Creativity.

courses.description: The students in this course must have already successfully completed Pre-Calculus Part I. This course is an in-depth review of polynomial, rational, exponential, and logarithmic functions, as well as an introduction to sequences and series. Each student is required to have a TI-83 or TI-84 graphing calculator. Any student that cannot acquire a calculator may be able to sign one out from the classroom for the duration of the school year.
courses.prerequisites: Final grade of B+ or higher in Algebra II, final grade of C or higher in Honors Algebra II, or teacher recommendation.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Effective Communication

courses.description: This course is designed for students who plan to study higher level math or science in their academic futures. Part I of this course focuses on trigonometry, specifically the six trigonometric functions and how they are applied with right triangles, oblique triangles, and how their graphs compare when translated. Students will prove various trigonometric identities, solve trigonometric equations, and utilize the Laws of Sine and Cosine to apply these calculations to real life situations. Each student is required to have a TI-83 or TI-84 graphing calculator. Any student that cannot acquire a calculator may be able to sign one out from the classroom for the duration of the school year.
courses.prerequisites: Final grade of C or higher in Pre-Calculus Part I or teacher recommendation.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Effective Communication

courses.description: This is an elective class for those juniors or seniors who may be concurrently taking an advanced science class or planning to pursue a college degree in a research field. Topics include constructing and summarizing single and multiple variable data, creating and conducting surveys and experiments, understanding randomness and probability principles, types of distributions (normal, binomial, geometric, student's t, chi-square), and inference (confidence intervals and hypothesis testing). Multiple software packages and presentation tools will be used and each student will be required to have a TI-84 graphing calculator. Students are required to take the Advanced Placement Examination in May.
courses.prerequisites: Final Grade of A- or higher in Algebra II or Algebra II Honors and teacher recommendation, or final grade of B or higher in Pre-Calculus I/Pre-Calculus II/Honors Pre-Calculus and teacher recommendation.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving, Effective Communication.

courses.description: This course integrates the review of basic math skills with practical knowledge students need to become informed financial decision-makers. Areas covered will include calculating wages, taxes, banking services, credit card buying, housing, and automobile purchases.
courses.prerequisites: The student must have two math credits and Junior or Senior class standing.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Personal Development.

courses.description: This course will cover mathematics material with an emphasis on money and finances. This is an applications-based learning approach that will include the stock market, modeling a business, banking services, credit cards, mortgages and loans. We will also explore automobile and home ownership, while including household budgeting. Also included will be a look at employment basics, commissions, benefits, Social Security, looking into retirement planning. The course includes a strong review of basic algebra formulas with variables, equations, functions, systems of equations, graphs and statistics. Selected advanced mathematics topics such as, piecewise functions, regression limits, exponential functions, and linear/quadratic systems are also addressed. Much of the daily computations will be spreadsheet and/or Desmos based. Students will learn how to program complex financial formulas and results. Proficiency is based on daily attitude, participation, quizzes, questions, tests, presentations, and projects.
courses.prerequisites: 12th grade standing and knowledge of functions.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical thinking and problem solving; Effective Communication; Personal Development.

courses.description: A semester course aimed at students who are curious about problem solving with mathematics. The course will introduce different types of mathematics that are not typically taught in high school; number theory, graph theory and probability. We will examine classic mathematics problems that sparked new mathematics into existence. Students will be responsible for taking notes and engaging on a daily basis. The final project will be student led with them answering a question of their own making while using their new mathematical models to answer them. We will be engaging in multiple levels of discussion and problem solving. Prerequisite: a strong desire to learn and solve problems with mathematics.
courses.prerequisites: 11th or 12th grade standing
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Critical Thinking and Problem Solving;

courses.description: This course is designed for those students who have successfully completed Algebra II and want to continue studying mathematics, and are interested in pursuing STEM careers at a more moderate pace than AP Statistics. Students will focus on statistical concepts such as displaying quantitative data, basic probability, confidence intervals and hypothesis testing.
courses.prerequisites: Completion of Algebra II or Honors Algebra II
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking and Problem Solving; Effective Communication.

courses.description: This course is designed for those students who have successfully completed Algebra II and want to continue studying mathematics, and are interested in pursuing STEM careers at a more moderate pace than Pre-Calculus. Students will review special right triangles and learn the definitions of the three primary trigonometric functions, their graphs, and their applications. Students will explore properties of the trigonometric functions using TI-84 graphing calculators and the online tool Desmos.
courses.prerequisites: Completion of Algebra II or Honors Algebra II
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking and Problem Solving; Effective Communication.

courses.description: This course blends lifelong physical activities with team activities and challenges students to be active and engaged. Students will be expected to demonstrate knowledge of concepts, principles, strategies and tactics related to a variety of movement patterns. Students will have an opportunity to experience many outdoor and indoor activities. The focus of a physically literate student in this course is to be able to demonstrate personal and social behavior that respects self and others. This is a proficiency based course and students are required to demonstrate proficiency in all learning outcomes.
courses.fulfills_text: Physical Education graduation requirement: 1.5 credits (at least 1.0 credit must be earned in BHS PE courses)
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement, Personal Development.

courses.description: This course introduces students to a wide range of individual lifetime sports that promote lifelong fitness, personal well-being, and active recreation. Through hands-on participation, skill development, and an understanding of foundational techniques, students will explore activities such as hiking, frisbee golf, badminton, pickleball, running, kayaking, and other low-impact or recreational sports suited for all ages.
courses.fulfills_text: Physical Education graduation requirement: 1.5 credits (at least 1.0 credit must be earned in BHS PE courses)
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Personal Development

courses.description: In this course, students will gain the skills and knowledge needed to participate in a variety of team sports and lifelong group activities; such as flag football, basketball, handball, soccer, ultimate, floor hockey and more. Students are encouraged to be active participants while creating a learning environment inclusive for all. Students will gain self-confidence while having fun through regular physical activity.
courses.fulfills_text: Physical Education graduation requirement: 1.5 credits (at least 1.0 credit must be earned in BHS PE courses)
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Personal Development

courses.description: Students will explore movement and dance as forms of lifelong physical activity. This is a non-traditional Physical Education class with a focus on understanding movement and movement patterns along with demonstrating concepts, principles, strategies and tactics related to movement and performance. Students will have an opportunity to experience some of the following activities: flexibility and stretching, HIIT, creative dance, Geo Fitness, aerobic activities, and more.
courses.fulfills_text: Physical Education graduation requirement: 1.5 credits (at least 1.0 credit must be earned in BHS PE courses)
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Personal Development

courses.description: This course is designed for students who want to learn how to improve their overall level of fitness to maintain a healthy lifestyle. Students will learn technical skills to perform a variety of fitness movements and gain the knowledge to create and implement an individualized fitness program. Topics covered include: goal setting, basic muscle structure & function, improving mobility, core development, cardiovascular fitness, Olympic lifts, strength training, programming, nutrition and recovery strategies for performance. Students will be assessed on active participation, fitness logs, current events, reflections, peer assessments, goal setting, fitness testing and a final project.
courses.fulfills_text: Physical Education graduation requirement: 1.5 credits (at least 1.0 credit must be earned in BHS PE courses)
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Personal Development

courses.description: Walking for Wellness encourages students to engage in structured walking-based activity and complementary wellness components (mobility, strength, nutrition, mindfulness, reflection). The course fosters lifelong physical activity habits, self-awareness of fitness and health, and the development of a personal wellness plan. The walking format provides accessibility and inclusivity for all students regardless of fitness level, while promoting alignment with physical literacy and Vermont’s wellness goals. Students will explore how walking supports physical, mental, and emotional well-being, and how to sustain healthy movement patterns beyond high school.
courses.fulfills_text: Physical Education graduation requirement: 1.5 credits (at least 1.0 credit must be earned in BHS PE courses)
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Personal Development

courses.description: Students may choose this course as an independent study for Physical Education. Students enrolled in this course have some flexibility of designing a plan that fits their needs. This course is ideal for those students who thrive with the opportunity to self-direct their own learning and wish to develop their own path and personal learning plan. There will be opportunities to do just that, while there will also be prescribed assignments. In this course students have the opportunity to use outside learning physical activity opportunities and apply them to this course for credit. The focus is becoming physically literate and demonstrating the knowledge and skills to achieve and maintain a health-enhancing level of physical activity and fitness. Regular meetings before school with a teacher and submissions of work will be required for students to demonstrate progress towards meeting course goals.
courses.prerequisites: Limited slots are available; student placement by teacher recommendation ONLY
courses.fulfills_text: Physical Education graduation requirement: Only 0.5 credit can be earned in PE Capstone.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Personal Development and Critical Thinking 52091, 52092, 52093

courses.description: Students may earn up to 0.5 PE credit for completing two seasons of interscholastic sports team involvement at BHS. This option is available beginning in sophomore year and ending Fall season of senior year. Students will fill out the interscholastic sports credit form and successfully complete their season. The coach and PE teacher overseeing this will determine successful completion. In addition, in order for students to receive this credit there are four required assignments that all student athletes must complete by the end of their season. Communication is given at the beginning of each season regarding this information. Students are assigned to a course in Schoology to access the assignments. In order to earn the credit, students must complete all five elements listed below: 1. Participation in the sport for the entire season 2. Weekly log of activities aligned with PE proficiencies 3. PE proficiency reflection 4. Coach and Student Rubric
courses.prerequisites: Students must earn at least 0.5 PE credit in their 9th grade yearOR be enrolled in a PE class in their 10th grade year (either semester)
courses.fulfills_text: Physical Education graduation requirement: 0.5 credits may be earned in Interscholastic Sports in Grades 10-12; Fall only, Senior Year.
courses.notes: Grades as printed: Grades 10-12 (Fall season only for 12th grade) | Primary Graduate Expectations: Personal Development

courses.description: Over the course of the semester, students will explore and engage in a variety of health related topics. They will gain factual information that can be used to make informed decisions regarding their own health. Topics covered include: mental health, nutrition, substance abuse & prevention, and sexual health. All units are aligned with the National Health Standards and each unit has specific learning outcomes and proficiencies. This course is a BHS and State graduation requirement.
courses.fulfills_text: This course is a BHS and State graduation requirement.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Cross-Cultural Understanding and Civic Engagement, Effective Communication, Personal Development; Curiosity and Creativity.

courses.description: In this fall semester course, students will investigate the food choices and practices of a region of our country, including: national issues such as diabetes, child hunger and heart disease. Students will plan, prepare and serve dishes related to his/her chosen area to the class. Students will also investigate and demonstrate understanding of food preparation and food science in chosen areas. The class will culminate with a holiday party for a chosen group. Unit evaluations will be class generated and include school wide contests.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Health
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Cross-Cultural Understanding and Civic Engagement, Personal Development.

courses.description: In this spring semester course, students will investigate the food choices and practices of an international culture or country, including global issues such as disasters, war, and other catastrophes and their effect on the food supply. Students will plan, prepare and serve dishes related to his/her chosen area to the class. Students will investigate and demonstrate understanding of food preparation and food science in chosen areas. Unit evaluations will be class generated and include school wide contests.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Health
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Cross-Cultural Understanding and Civic Engagement, Personal Development.

courses.description: This course provides students with scientific literacy in earth sciences. These areas will be explored through inquiry, discussion, projects, lab investigations, research and technology. This course will include place-based study of the Burlington area, from the ecology of Lake Champlain to the geology of Lone Rock Point. Students have the option to earn honors credit in this class by demonstrating learning of key concepts, skills, and knowledge, on identified assignments and assessments throughout the school year at an honors level; the earned honors designation will be awarded at the end of the year. This course is required for all 9th grade students. 10th grade students by teacher recommendation only. This course is not appropriate for 11-12th grade students.
courses.fulfills_text: This course is required for all 9th grade students. | Science dept table: Required Courses - Earth Systems Science (9th grade)
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication, Creativity and Curiosity, Critical Thinking and Problem Solving.

courses.description: This full-year course focuses on Biology and biological applications and will help to improve the student’s science skills, as well as general academic skills. Students will regularly conduct laboratory investigations and complete research projects. The major biological content covered will include biochemistry, cell structures and functions, cellular energy systems, cellular reproduction, genetics, evolution, and environmental science. Successful completion of this course will provide students with the skills needed to take future science courses.
courses.prerequisites: Enrollment in grade 10 or higher.
courses.fulfills_text: Science dept table: Required Courses - Biology (10th grade)
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication, Creativity and Curiosity, Critical Thinking and Problem Solving.

courses.description: Biology is the study of life. In this class, students will do the following: ● Study how environmental changes drive the evolution of a species ● Use models and simulations to uncover how DNA encodes all the instructions for making living things and research how mistakes in those instructions can lead to a variety of disorders such as cancer ● Explore how the body changes during intense exercise like running a marathon In Honors Biology, students will continue to expand their proficiency in science skills such as Asking Questions and Developing Models (ESS proficiencies). Students will also be asked to show proficiency in Analyzing and Interpreting Data, Mathematics and Computational Thinking, and Engaging in Argument from Evidence. Students will show proficiency in these skills through modeling current biological concepts, engaging in scientific discussion, exploring current scientific writing, conducting labs, applying technology and simulations to expand understanding, writing scientific explanations, and completing research and projects. Students’ biology-specific content knowledge will also be assessed throughout the course using quizzes and tests. This challenging and fast-paced course will provide students the skills needed to take future honors and AP-level science classes at BHS and introductory college-level science courses in the future.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Earth Systems Science and Earth Systems Science teacher recommendation.
courses.fulfills_text: Science dept table: Required Courses - Biology (10th grade)
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication, Creativity and Curiosity, Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: This proficiency based college preparatory chemistry class focuses on proficiency in fundamental chemistry concepts and skills. This course includes a mixture of classic laboratory work, guided inquiry, and experimental design. A strong algebra foundation is essential for success as it is applied to many chemistry concepts. Topics studied include: classification of matter, atoms, elements, nuclear chemistry, chemical compounds, bonding, chemical composition, and reactions.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion or concurrent enrollment of Biology I, Integrated Math 1 (or a higher level math), and recommendation of current science teacher
courses.fulfills_text: Science dept table: Required Courses - Chemistry and or / Physics (10th, 11th, or 12th grade)
courses.notes: Grades as printed: Grades 11-12, 10th Grade by Recommendation | Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Creativity & Curiosity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: This college preparatory chemistry class is a rigorous, math-dependent science course. Basic chemistry concepts are emphasized in class discussions, labs, and independent learning. Topics studied include: atomic and molecular structure/ theory, periodic law, chemical bonding, formulas, equations and stoichiometry, chemical reactions, acid and bases, and nuclear chemistry.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of or concurrent enrollment in Biology I or Biology I Honors, Algebra II or Algebra II Honors, and recommendation of current science teacher.
courses.fulfills_text: Science dept table: Required Courses - Chemistry and or / Physics (10th, 11th, or 12th grade)
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication, Creativity & Curiosity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: This is a college-preparatory laboratory oriented physics course designed for students with strong reading, problem solving and computation skills. Topics in physics include Energy, Newton’s Laws, Gravitation, Waves, and Sound. Topics are covered using inquiry, group work, experimentation, and mathematical relationships as indicated by the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS).
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion or concurrent enrollment of Biology I, Integrated Math 1 (or a higher level math), and recommendation of current science teache . r
courses.fulfills_text: Science dept table: Required Courses - Chemistry and or / Physics (10th, 11th, or 12th grade)
courses.notes: Grades as printed: Grades 11-12, 10th Grade by Recommendation | Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Effective Communication.

courses.description: This math and laboratory-based course is designed for students with very strong reading, problem solving, and mathematics skills. Students work independently and in collaborative groups to discover important concepts in the study of kinematics, Newton’s Laws, energy, rotational motion, waves, sound, and optics.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of or concurrent enrollment in Biology I or Biology I Honors, Algebra II or Algebra II Honors, and recommendation of current science teacher.
courses.fulfills_text: Science dept table: Required Courses - Chemistry and or / Physics (10th, 11th, or 12th grade)

courses.description: Advanced Placement Biology is an advanced, honors level biology program. Topics studied include biochemistry, cellular biology, cell cycle and communication, heredity, gene expression, evolution, and ecology. It is equivalent to 2 semesters of college biology. Depending on the college or university attended, students who do well on the AP exam can earn up to 8 college credits. Students should have a strong background in mathematics and should be proficient in the use of basic laboratory equipment and be familiar with laboratory safety procedures. Students in the course will take the Advanced Placement Examination in Biology given in May of each year. The running of this course is dependent upon sufficient enrollment and staffing.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Biology I, Chemistry I, and Algebra II, and recommendation from current science teacher.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Effective Communication.

courses.description: This is a challenging, mathematical, laboratory-oriented chemistry course designed for those students with interest in expanding their chemistry knowledge. Topics include extensions of ideas learned in Chemistry I, inorganic chemistry, introduction to organic chemicals, analytical methods, thermochemistry, and chemical kinetics and equilibrium. The class meets for 2 Blocks, is equivalent to 2 semesters of college Chemistry, and can earn up to 8 college credits. Students will take the AP Chemistry Exam in May. The running of this course is dependent upon sufficient enrollment and staffing.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Algebra II & Chemistry I or Chemistry I Honors and recommendation from current science teacher.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication, Creativity and Curiosity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: Students will study the interrelated parts and connections between earth systems and human impact upon them through laboratory exercises, modeling, debate and independent research. National and local environmental policy, planning, and impact are also explored in depth. Students will study these and other topics in order to prepare for the Advanced Placement exam in May. The course is equivalent to 1 semester of college Environmental Science. Depending on the college or university attended, students who do well on the AP exam can earn up to 4 college credits.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Integrated Math I or Geometry, concurrent enrollment in or successful completion of Biology 1 or Honors Biology, and recommendation from current science teacher.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication, Creativity and Curiosity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: This semester-long class takes an in-depth look at the chemical and biological processes that occur when cooking and fermenting food. We also learn the proper techniques that determine a recipe’s success. We usually make the following foods: jams, salsa, biscuits, frying foods such as french fries and cider donuts, yogurt, homemade cider, and sauerkraut. We learn how to grill food and work in the school garden harvesting food. Finally, you will choose a recipe to cook and investigate as a final project.
courses.prerequisites: 10th-11th graders should be concurrently enrolled in biology, chemistry or physics
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication, Creativity and Curiosity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: Cookies, cakes, bread, sourdough, chocolate souffles, eggs, meats, grilling, pancakes, waffles, maple syrup and sugaring. This semester will have you baking, cooking, grilling and tapping maple trees producing the best foods all based on proven scientific techniques. Once the snow begins to melt we head out to tap the maple trees and boil off the sap to use on the best pancakes and waffles that you create. Finally, we end the year learning how to grill savory meats and vegetables in the beautiful Vermont spring outdoors.
courses.prerequisites: 10th-11th graders should be concurrently enrolled in biology, chemistry or physics.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication, Creativity and Curiosity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

courses.description: Human Anatomy and Physiology is a challenging year-long course that encompasses the parts of the body and how they work. This course is designed for students who wish to learn how their bodies work or are interested in pursuing careers in the health field after graduation. Topics studied will include the following systems: integumentary (skin), skeletal, muscular, digestive, nervous, cardiovascular, endocrine, and reproductive. Four optional dissections aid in our discovery of the human body.
courses.prerequisites: Concurrent enrollment in or successful completion of Biology.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Effective Communication.

courses.description: This course aims to provide students with an appreciation and basic working knowledge of our oceans and marine life. The course will focus on both the living and nonliving components in our oceans that contribute to the diverse ecosystems and abundant resources under the sea! In addition to natural ocean phenomena such as currents, tides, plate tectonics, island formation, species diversity and weather, human impacts like pollution, over exploitation of fishing/whaling practices, climate change, and possible career fields will be studied. Demonstrations, labs, videos, and group projects will enhance learning from classroom lectures, articles, and group discussions.
courses.prerequisites: Completion of or concurrently enrolled in Biology
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking and Problem Solving; Effective Communication.

courses.description: This semester-long course will introduce students to pathogens that cause human and/or animal disease. Emphasis will be on viral, bacterial, protozoan, and fungal diseases. Students will learn to classify microbes using taxonomic hierarchy. Animal defense mechanisms, disease progression and disease transmission will be primary topics of study. We will review the human response to disease over the centuries. The laboratory component of this course will focus on the basic methods to cultivate, identify and control pathogenic microbial growth.
courses.prerequisites: Completion of or concurrently enrolled in Biology
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking and Problem Solving; Effective Communication; Creativity and Curiosity.

courses.description: This semester-long course will introduce students to the field of parasitology. Topics will include parasite diversity, life cycles, host defense mechanisms, and host disease. Biology concepts of immunology, ecology, and evolution will weave throughout our course. Methods for parasite control and treatments with antiparasitic medicines will be explored. The laboratory component of this course will examine and classify parasites of medical and veterinary importance using light microscopy.
courses.prerequisites: Completion of or concurrently enrolled in Biology
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking and Problem Solving; Effective Communication; Creativity and Curiosity.

courses.description: Take advantage of this opportunity for a second year of high school physics. Topics include astronomy, optics and light, electricity, magnetism, relativity and other modern topics. Students should have strong reading and math skills and be able to work well in collaborative groups, as well as independently.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Physics I or Honors Physics I and concurrent enrollment in or completion of Precalculus, and recommendation of Honors Physics II teacher.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Effective Communication

courses.description: This course is designed for students who are interested in exploring the cultures of the world languages offered at BHS. This course provides students with an introduction in English to the geography, the culture and to some history of the countries of the languages taught at BHS. The emphasis of the course is not so much on language acquisition but rather on the exploration of cultural topics. The objective of the course is for students to gain some cultural awareness and to gain readiness for any level 1 of world language class at BHS.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

courses.description: An introduction to the French language and culture, this course offers the building blocks of second language acquisition through the alphabet, number system, basic grammar structures and vocabulary. Students learn to communicate about themselves in such areas as family, school, leisure activities, clothes, etc. and their surroundings. They can identify cultural objects, images, and symbols, and contributions of the target culture. Knowledge in other subject areas (math, social studies, art, etc) is reinforced. Students can identify differences in language and cultural patterns and can identify the target language in their daily lives. They will begin to develop the ability to greet and respond to greetings, introduce and respond to introductions, engage in conversations, express likes and dislikes, make requests, obtain information, understand some ideas and begin to provide information. They can expect to speak in short sentences of directed dialogues, to write simple sentences, to read short passages for comprehension and to listen to patterns of conversations. Stage I proficiency is assessed during the year.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

courses.description: This course is designed for students who successfully completed level 1 and/or achieved the necessary scoring on the placement exam. Content topics of French 1 are explored in depth. New vocabulary is introduced through authentic and cultural readings. The focus of the texts is the French-speaking world. Cultural behaviors and practices throughout the French-speaking world are studied and discussed. New grammar is practiced regularly in order to improve sentence structure. Conversational skills and practical vocabulary are used daily in class activities. Progress is assessed throughout the year.
courses.prerequisites: B- or higher in French 1 and/or recommendation of middle/high school French 1 teacher
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

courses.description: At the third level students continue to acquire skills leading to greater proficiency. Content topics of French 1 and 2 are explored in more depth. Students develop the ability to make requests; express their needs; understand and express important ideas and some detail; describe and compare; and use and understand expressions indicating emotion. They will be able to create simple paragraphs when writing; understand important ideas and some details in highly contextualized authentic texts when reading; and use and understand learned expressions, sentences, and strings of sentences, questions, and polite commands when speaking and listening. Progress is assessed throughout the year. Students may participate in the school’s travel/language trip to France.
courses.prerequisites: B- or higher in French 2, successful completion of French 2 final exam and/or French 2 teacher recommendation
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

courses.description: Students may elect to continue their study of French language and French culture through this course, which continues to foster the enhancement of communication skills through expanding upon the foundations for verbal, listening and writing skills laid in previous French courses. The curriculum focuses on reading, writing, listening and speaking French in class with peers and the teacher and understanding the culture. This will be done by incorporating different strategies in which students will be expected to participate: writing activities, creating projects, and engaging in the target language through music and videos/film.
courses.prerequisites: B- or higher in French 3 and/or recommendation of French 3 teacher
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

courses.description: In French 5 students increase their knowledge and improve their proficiency engaging in meaningful communication. Pronunciation, expressions, vocabulary and grammar topics are reviewed and practiced using a variety of authentic resources including music, recordings, films, literature excerpts, newspapers and magazines. Skills developed include ability to clarify understanding, express and understand opinions, narrate and understand narration, and identify, state, and understand feelings and emotions. Students read, analyze and engage in class debates, write essays, reflections and reactions, give and critique presentations, present skits and role-play activities, and complete written and oral projects. The course is conducted entirely in French. Students may participate in the school’s travel and language trip to France.
courses.prerequisites: B- or higher in French 4 and/or recommendation of French 4 teacher
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

courses.description: Students in this introductory course begin to develop: the ability to greet and respond to greetings, introduce and respond to introductions, engage in conversations, express likes and dislikes, make requests, obtain information, understand some ideas and familiar details. In addition students will provide information about topics pertaining to the self and others, family, friends, home, school, schedules, and leisure activities. They can identify Hispanic cultural perspectives and practices beyond the school setting, make connections between Spanish and other disciplines they study, and identify similarities and differences between Hispanic and English language and behaviors. Spanish I students begin to speak in short sentences of directed dialogues, write simple sentences, read short passages enhanced with visual clues and understand some ideas and familiar details presented in clear, uncomplicated speech when listening. Progress is assessed throughout the year.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

courses.description: This course is designed for students who have successfully completed Spanish 1 and/or achieved the necessary standard on the placement exam. Content topics of Spanish I are explored in more depth. Cultural behaviors are studied and practiced. Authentic materials, intended for native speakers, are introduced. Students are able to participate in school-wide multicultural activities in Spanish. Proficiency is assessed throughout the year.
courses.prerequisites: B- or higher in Spanish 1 and/or recommendation of middle/high school Spanish teacher
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

courses.description: In Spanish 3, students continue to acquire skills leading to proficiency at Stage II. Content topics of Spanish 1 and 2 are explored in more depth. Students develop the ability to make requests, express their needs, understand and express important ideas and some detail, describe and compare, and use and understand expressions indicating emotion. They will be able to create simple paragraphs when writing, understand important ideas and some details in highly contextualized authentic texts when reading, and use and understand learned expressions, sentences, and strings of sentences, questions, and polite commands when speaking and listening. Progress is assessed throughout the year.
courses.prerequisites: B- or higher in Spanish 2 and successful completion of Spanish 2 final exam and/or recommendation of Spanish 2 teacher
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

courses.description: Students may elect to continue their study of the Spanish language and Hispanic culture through this course which fosters the enhancement of communication skills through expanding content and higher expectations. The course is conducted almost entirely in Spanish. The content will range from self-related topics (family, friends, home, school, activities, likes and dislikes, shopping, clothes, and pets) through less personal concerns (geography, history, directions, weather, cultural/historical figures, places and events, transportation and travel, food and eating customs, and work/professions), to broader topics culturally pertinent to the target language (art, literature, ). music, current affairs, and civilization Students begin to analyze cultural behaviors, recognize and use idiomatic expressions, and interact appropriately in realistic situations. Proficiency is assessed throughout the year.
courses.prerequisites: B- or higher in Spanish 3 and/or recommendation of a Spanish teacher.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

courses.description: In this course, students have intensive exposure to wide ranging and demanding content where high expectations and demanding standards in all skill areas and in all aspects of scholarship will be the rule. Content will range from that delineated for Spanish 4, through topics of broader cultural significance such as the educational system, the government, and political and social issues. Skills developed include the ability to explain and clarify understanding, express and understand opinions, narrate and understand narration in the present, past, and future, and identify, state, and understand feelings and emotions. When speaking, students use strings of related sentences; when writing, they can create simple paragraphs; when reading, they can acquire knowledge and new information from comprehensive, authentic texts; and when listening, they are able to understand most spoken language when the message is deliberately and carefully conveyed by a speaker accustomed to dealing with learners. Preparation for the Advanced Placement examination in Spanish begins at this level. The course is entirely conducted in Spanish.
courses.prerequisites: B- or higher in Spanish 4 and/or recommendation of a Spanish teacher.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

courses.description: This course is designed for heritage Spanish speakers — students who grew up speaking Spanish in informal settings but may not have had formal instruction. It builds on existing language skills to strengthen reading, writing, and grammar, while expanding vocabulary and cultural awareness. Students will improve their ability to use Spanish confidently in both academic and real-world contexts.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

courses.description: Latin I exposes students to the language, culture, and history of the Romans. An introduction to the language through the Cambridge Series emphasizes comprehension of the Latin language by reading it and thus understanding the social and political history of the Romans, especially during the first Century AD. The year will focus on Pompeii, the city buried by Mt. Vesuvius in A.D. 79. A variety of cultural topics are explored including family life, entertainment, education, food, slavery, art and architecture (through slide presentations), and religion. In addition, students become familiar with the geography of the ancient world and study the relationship of Latin vocabulary to English. The result of the student’s study of Latin is improved knowledge of both English vocabulary and grammar, an expanded understanding of the relationship of the ancient world to his or her own, and an appreciation for other foreign languages and cultures.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

courses.description: The Cambridge Series pursues readings in philosophy, engineering, the legionary soldier, and religion. The Romans abroad in the West, i.e. Britain, and in the East, i.e. Masada, offers further study of social and historical topics. Students will read about Rome during the reign of Domitian and study the art and architecture of the city of Rome with emphasis on the Roman Forum. Students will also study the role of the legionary soldier in the empire. Vergil’s great epic the Aeneid is read in English providing students with a knowledge of the mythology connected with Rome’s foundation. The student will work on mastery of the language by acquisition and understanding of advanced grammar and reading Latin in the original.
courses.prerequisites: Completion Latin II and/or recommendation of the Latin teacher
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

courses.description: Students in this introductory course begin to develop the ability to greet and respond to greetings, introduce and respond to introductions, engage in conversations, express likes and dislikes, make requests, obtain information, and understand some ideas and familiar details. In addition, students begin to provide information about topics pertaining to themselves and others: family, friends, home, school and schedules, leisure activities, etc. They can identify German cultural perspectives and practices beyond the school setting, make connections between German and other disciplines they study, and identify similarities and differences between German and English language and behaviors. German I students begin to speak in short sentences of directed dialogues, to write simple sentences, to read short passages enhanced with visual clues and understand some ideas and familiar details presented in clear, uncomplicated speech when listening. Progress is assessed throughout the year.
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

courses.description: This course is designed for students who have successfully completed German 1. Content topics of German I are explored in more depth. The topics are designed to steer the student to express opinions, ask questions, and participate in simulations of real-life situations.The course is project based in nature where students will use their growing knowledge of German to design and present their notion of the ideal school, compose hip hop music, create board games and even film video projects of an original German comedy series. Other real-life topics are concerned with everyday life such as shopping for groceries and planning meals, purchasing gifts, discussing free time activities and hobbies, eating in restaurants, and finding one's way in a German city. Short stories, poems, films, and cultural readings all help students to further improve their reading, listening and speaking skills. Authentic materials, intended for native speakers, are introduced. Students are able to participate in school-wide multicultural activities in German. Progress is assessed throughout the year.
courses.prerequisites: B- or higher in German 1 and/or recommendation of the German teacher
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

courses.description: In this course, students continue to acquire proficiency skills, and the content topics of German 1 and 2 are explored in more depth. Subjects such as children’s literature (Grimm’s fairy tales), German history in the 20th century, German politics, German film history, etc. are analyzed and discussed in depth. Students also begin to read, discuss, and debate topics introduced in contemporary literature, including short stories by such authors as Brecht, Borchert and Bichsel. This course is similar to German 2 in that it is project based where, for example, students compose and film their own endings to fairy tales, create their own cooking show, and even organize a German Film festival for the whole school with post-film “talk-backs” organized by students in German 3. Students develop the ability to make requests, express their needs, understand and express important ideas in some detail, describe and compare, and use and understand expressions indicating emotion. They will be able to create simple paragraphs when writing, understand important ideas and some details in highly contextualized authentic texts when reading, and use and understand learned expressions, sentences, and strings of sentences, questions, and polite commands when speaking and listening. Progress is assessed throughout the year.
courses.prerequisites: B- or higher in German 2 and/or recommendation of the German teacher
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

courses.description: This course continues to foster the enhancement of communication skills through expanding content and grammatical knowledge. Although this course is somewhat organic in that students will be able to help come up with topics they are passionate about at the outset of the year, there are some core topics that will be discussed. For example, students will explore literature, cinema history, and culture, the financial and economic world, environmental concerns and human creativity. Literary works ranging from poetry and short stories, sections of Goethe's Faust to Rilke's poems and Durrenmatt’s post WWII works, generate many opportunities for projects, debates and discussions. A unit on literature, art, and music of the Holocaust, as well as the study of propaganda and its influence on the youth of Germany, is offered during the second semester. This unit includes guest lectures from Holocaust survivors of concentration camps and professors from the UVM departments of Hebrew, German, and Russian. Students begin to analyze cultural behaviors, recognize and use idiomatic expressions, and interact appropriately in realistic situations. Progress is assessed throughout the year.
courses.prerequisites: B- or higher in German 3 and/or recommendation of the German teacher
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

courses.description: This is a college level course designed to prepare students for success on the AP German Language and Culture exam. Students will continue their exploration of the language, history, culture and practices of the German-speaking world, and will be encouraged to make comparisons and connections with their own culture throughout the year. This course will be taught almost exclusively in German, and students will be required to participate using the target language. Students will engage in activities and assignments focused on Interpersonal, Interpretive, and Presentational modes of communication . As a class, we will address the following interdisciplinary themes of the AP exam in German: Global Challenges, Science and Technology, Contemporary Life, Personal and Public Identities, Families and Communities, and Beauty and Aesthetics . Course materials include authentic reading materials, German video clips, films and podcasts made for a native speaker audience addressing these interdisciplinary themes.
courses.prerequisites: B- or higher in German 3 and/or recommendation of the German teacher
courses.notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

courses.description: This class is an introduction to philosophy. We'll talk about ethics, personal identity, and some other topics that we come up with together. There'll be roughly one reading per week, sometimes from philosophy books but other times from magazines or short stories. Assessment will be mostly short writing assignments.

courses.description: Program Description The Burlington City & Lake Semester (BCL) is an intensive semester program that offers students the opportunity to use the city as their classroom and curriculum for one semester of their high school journey. Students will dedicate their entire Blue Day schedule to explore real world issues, build deeper relationships with a diverse group of 20 peers, and take action alongside adults to improve the community. BCL participants are ambitious and excited for the deeper, student-centered learning that is possible in an experiential program. The curriculum features a cross-disciplinary exploration of five core themes through four units of study. Students may earn one half (0.5) credit each in English and Social Studies, as well as one (1.0) elective credit in Applied Research upon successful completion of BCL. Applications may be submitted here and more information can be found at btvcityandlake.org. *Please note that only the 0.5 English credit is NCAA-approved.

courses.description: Deeper Learning allows students in 10th, 11th, or 12th grade to focus on a specific topic that is not otherwise available at BHS or for students who want to deepen their learning and understanding of content they have been exposed to in a previously completed class. This learning experience will provide all students the opportunity to design in-depth studies based on their interests and passions. These student-designed studies should align with the five Graduation Expectations, which include: cross-cultural understanding and civic engagement, effective communication, critical thinking and problem solving, curiosity and creativity, and personal development. Students may complete Deeper Learning for either core or elective credit in a 0.5 or 1.0 (one-half or one credit) increment maximum in their high school enrollment. The student must identify a minimum of two Graduation Expectations that will align with the study’s objectives. Deeper Learning is available per teacher contract availability. Independent Study courses should not duplicate current offerings and must be supervised by a content area teacher. Students in good academic standing may discuss this option with their School Counselor. Eligible students will then identify a faculty advisor who is appropriately licensed and meet with this personnel to complete an Independent Study Contract together; the student will return this contract to the School Counselor for approval. Please note that while a teacher must agree to serve as an advisor, and be present for the demonstration of learning at the end of the study, no teacher is obligated to serve in this capacity. Only an appropriately licensed teacher advisor can evaluate the demonstration of learning and issue a recommendation as to whether credit should be earned by the student. Final approval and credit award determinations will be made by the Director of School Counseling and/or Principal. Please note: an Independent Study in music will not satisfy requirements for the VYO or state, regional, or national music festivals and organizations.

courses.description: SUCCEED is an alternative general education program for 9th and 10th grade students designed to provide holistic staff support in a smaller community setting within the larger BHS campus. Subject based classes are provided in a self-contained classroom, with a focus on the mastery of essential skills in core content areas. Students have scheduled break times throughout the 3.5 hours program span. Students who complete the program and work expectations can earn up to four (4) credits over the course of the year, one (1) in each of the following core content areas: Math, English, Science and Social Studies. Students will be enrolled in electives, as needed, in conjunction with this program. SUCCEED students will be awarded credit on a quarterly basis to reflect work completion and skill mastery, in increments of one-quarter credit (0.25). Entry into this program requires referral to and approval from the BHS Succeed team.

courses.description: The LINK program is a small school-based community for students serviced through an Individualized Education Plan (IEP) who require enhanced executive functioning, social-emotional, and academic support throughout their regularly scheduled school day. LINK provides alternative pathways to graduation as well as proactive planning on post-graduate transitions into the community. In LINK, students have the opportunity to continue to practice the application of skills in core course assignments with individualized tutorial support within a structured small classroom environment. Entry into this program requires a referral from a school-based team at BHS.
courses.notes: program

courses.description: The Bridging Program is a dual-year commitment, nine (9) hours a week at Champlain Community Services that offers students the opportunity to participate with a cohort of peers from across other school districts in Chittenden County. They develop transitional life skills, including career exploration, community connections, independent living, and self advocacy skills in a supportive environment. Participants engage with community partners and businesses to learn about government, society, culture, environment, finances, and other topics related to student interests and life after high school. A certified teacher in a specific content area will serve as an advisor to the student and provide demonstrations of learning through an independent study model. A student can earn one (1.0) academic credit for each year of participation, as determined by a Special Education team, as well as potential elective credit(s). Entry into this program requires a referral from a school-based team at BHS.

courses.description: Students demonstrating self motivation and the ability to be successful in an asynchronous learning environment may have the opportunity to take online classes through the Vermont Virtual Learning Collaborative (VTVLC ). BHS is provided with a designated number of VTVLC “traditional” and “on demand” course slots each year. Enrollment in a VTVLC course is based on the collective School Counseling department prioritization of need and equitable access to this limited resource. Students and families may also opt for self-pay. See the VTVLC website for semester and full-year options. Interested students should meet with their School Counselor to discuss how to incorporate these choices into their course enrollment and graduation plan.

courses.description: Dual enrollment classes provide BHS students the opportunity to access rigorous college courses. Successful students demonstrate responsibility for their own learning, work completion, and communication with the instructor. Students are eligible to enroll once a minimum of twelve (12) high school credits have been earned. Dual enrollment courses must be completed prior to graduation to be awarded credit. Students may need to meet additional course prerequisites prior to enrollment, including taking the Accuplacer Test. Vermont provides two tuition vouchers for 11th and 12th grade students to take classes for both high school and college credit. The vouchers cover tuition only; all additional materials and fees are the responsibility of the student. A student/family unable to cover the cost of materials and fees should inform their school counselor, as BHS seeks to minimize barriers posed by financial need. If a student has already used both dual enrollment vouchers, and would like to take additional college course work, they may independently apply to the Community College of Vermont (CCV) and assume financial responsibility for tuition and fees.

A culminating showcase allows students, parents, and community members to learn from each other and celebrate YES accomplishments. Students will sign up during the third academic quarter and informed of their courses in the spring. Information on the current year’s offerings can be found on the BHS website.
